lead: A point-to-point link is one transmitter, one fiber path and one receiver, and nothing else between them. It exists because most real systems are exactly that: a trunk between two telephone exchanges, a cable-TV headend feeding a node, a 10 km run across a campus. The same five blocks serve both link types. What changes is the question asked at the end. A digital link carries bits and is judged by how many arrive wrong. An analog link carries a waveform and is judged by how much noise rides on it. That one difference drives the whole design.
prereq: You need Unit 3 (sources and power launching) and Unit 4 (photodiodes, receiver sensitivity, bit error rate).

sections.h3: The five blocks of a point-to-point link

blocks.text: The signal path is fixed: light leaves the source, loses power in the fiber, lands on a photodiode, is amplified, and is judged. Draw it once and both link types fit the same drawing.

items: Source and driver. An LED or laser diode plus the circuit that pumps current into it. In a digital link the driver sends current pulses; in an analog link it sends a continuously varying current. The output is modulated optical power.
Fiber with splices and connectors. The cable plus every joint on the route. Each joint adds a fixed loss, and the run adds αL, where α is the attenuation in dB/km and L is the length in km.
Photodiode. Converts optical power P to current I = R·P, where R is the responsivity in A/W.
Preamplifier and filter. Raises the small current to a usable level and limits the bandwidth. That bandwidth decides how much noise arrives along with the signal.

Decision circuit or measurement stage. In a digital link it samples the filtered pulse at the centre of the bit and decides 1 or 0. In an analog link the output is kept as a waveform and measured for carrier-to-noise ratio.

blocks.text: Every loss before the photodiode simply reduces the current. Noise added by the preamplifier sets a floor that no later stage can remove; the only cure is more received optical power.

For a digital link the design settles four numbers. Bit rate B, in bits/s, sets the bandwidth the receiver must pass and the rise time the pulse is allowed. Distance L, in km, sets the loss αL. Received power P_rx, in dBm or watts, must stay above the receiver sensitivity for the required error rate. Pulse shape must still be open at the sampling instant after the fiber has broadened it.

The score card is the bit error rate, BER: the fraction of bits decided wrongly. A target of 10⁻⁹ means one error per thousand million bits, the usual telephony-class figure. At 2.5 Gbit/s that is roughly one error every 0.4 s. BER falls very steeply as received power rises, so a link either clears its target with margin or fails badly; there is little middle ground.

In practice you check two budgets. The power budget asks whether enough light arrives. The rise-time budget asks whether the pulse is still sharp enough. The link passes only if both do, and the shorter of the two limits wins. Power usually limits long links; rise time usually limits fast ones.

sections.h3: Analog link: linear modulation and carrier-to-noise ratio

blocks.text: In an analog link the light intensity follows the waveform itself, so the source must be modulated linearly. The modulation index m, no unit, is the peak swing of the optical power divided by its mean value. One fiber may carry a single video channel or many subcarriers, each a narrow band placed at a different frequency.

blocks.where: CNR is a power ratio, no unit; m is the modulation index (no unit); I is the mean photocurrent in amperes; i_n is the total RMS noise current in amperes inside the channel bandwidth. Both currents are squared, so their units cancel. In decibels, CNR(dB) = 10 log₁₀ CNR.

blocks.text: The signal current is an RMS value, mI/√2, so its power is (mI)²/2 in A². The noise power is i_n², where i_n collects shot noise, the thermal noise of the preamplifier and any relative intensity noise of the source. Widening the filter raises i_n in proportion to the square root of bandwidth, so CNR drops.

Noise is only half the analog story. When two or more subcarriers share the fiber, the square-law detector mixes them. Sums and differences of two carriers give second-order beats, quoted as composite second order (CSO). Combinations of three give third-order beats, quoted as composite triple beat (CTB). Both land inside channels and cannot be filtered out. Dynamic range is the useful span of m, from the CNR floor at the bottom to the distortion ceiling at the top.

blocks.text: Fix the measure before you design. A digital power budget starts from the receiver sensitivity written for a stated BER. An analog budget starts from the CNR the customer needs at the far end, and then checks that the modulation index chosen stays below the distortion limit.

examples.question: An analog link carries one 6 MHz video channel at 0.85 μm. The received optical power is −20 dBm, the photodiode responsivity is 0.5 A/W, the modulation index is m = 0.7, and the total RMS noise current in the 6 MHz band is 5 nA. Find the mean photocurrent, the RMS signal current and the CNR in dB.
steps: Convert the optical power out of dBm. P = 10^(−20/10) mW = 0.01 mW = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ W.
Mean photocurrent: I = R·P = 0.5 A/W × 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ W = 5.0 × 10⁻⁶ A = 5 μA.
RMS signal current: mI/√2 = 0.7 × 5 μA ÷ 1.414 = 3.5 ÷ 1.414 = 2.475 μA.
Signal power in the channel: (2.475 μA)² = 6.125 μA².
Noise current 5 nA = 0.005 μA, so noise power = (0.005 μA)² = 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ μA².
CNR = 6.125 ÷ 2.5 × 10⁻⁵ = 2.45 × 10⁵. Working both currents in μA keeps the ratio unitless.
examples.answer: Mean photocurrent 5 μA, RMS signal current 2.475 μA, and CNR = 2.45 × 10⁵, that is 53.9 dB.
examples.check:
import math

P_dBm = -20.0
P_mW = 10 ** (P_dBm / 10)
R = 0.5
I_uA = R * P_mW * 1e-3 * 1e6
m = 0.7
i_sig_uA = m * I_uA / math.sqrt(2)
p_sig = i_sig_uA ** 2
i_n_uA = 5e-9 * 1e6
p_noise = i_n_uA ** 2
cnr = p_sig / p_noise
cnr_dB = 10 * math.log10(cnr)

print(round(I_uA, 4))
print(round(i_sig_uA, 4))
print(round(p_sig, 4))
print(round(p_noise, 8))
print(round(cnr, 1))
print(round(cnr_dB, 2))

traps: dBm is optical power, not current. Convert to mW or W first, then multiply by responsivity in A/W. Multiplying a dBm figure straight by R is the commonest slip.
Signal is an RMS current, so divide the peak mI by √2 before squaring. Noise adds in power, not in current: never add a signal current and a noise current as plain numbers.
CNR is a power ratio, so it goes to dB with 10 log₁₀. Using 20 log₁₀ doubles the answer and looks plausible.
CSO and CTB are distortion, not noise. Adding more received power lifts CNR but leaves the beat products sitting right where they were, relative to the carrier.
Examiners like the pair BER and CNR side by side. Remember BER belongs to a decision on bits and CNR to a continuous waveform; a link can pass one and fail the other.

quiz.q: Name the five blocks of a point-to-point link in order.
quiz.a: Source and driver, fiber with splices and connectors, photodiode, preamplifier and filter, decision circuit (or measurement stage).

quiz.q: Which measure judges a digital link and which judges an analog link?
quiz.a: BER for the digital link; CNR, along with CSO, CTB and dynamic range, for the analog link.

quiz.q: Why does widening the receiver filter lower the CNR of an analog link?
quiz.a: RMS noise current rises as the square root of bandwidth, so noise power i_n² rises in proportion to bandwidth, while the signal power (mI)²/2 stays the same. CNR therefore falls.

quiz.q: An analog receiver gets −13 dBm and the photodiode responsivity is 0.8 A/W. Find the mean photocurrent.
A channel has m = 0.5, mean photocurrent 10 μA and RMS noise current 10 nA. Find the CNR in dB.
quiz.a: Signal current = 0.5 × 10 ÷ 1.414 = 3.54 μA, so signal power = 12.5 μA². Noise power = (0.01 μA)² = 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ μA². CNR = 1.25 × 10⁵, that is 51.0 dB.

quiz.q: Raising the modulation index improves CNR. Why is it still kept modest in a multi-channel subcarrier link?
quiz.a: Signal power grows as m² but CSO also grows about m² and CTB about m³. Past a point the beat products fall inside the channels and cannot be filtered, so the distortion ceiling, not the noise floor, sets the limit.

quiz.q: A digital link meets its BER target at half the specified distance but fails at full distance. Which of the four system considerations changed, and how would you check?
quiz.a: Received power fell by the extra loss αL, so the current into the preamplifier dropped below the sensitivity needed for the target BER; dispersion may also have closed the pulse. Check the power budget first, then the rise-time budget, and fix whichever fails.

beyond: Not for the exam. Analog optical links never disappeared: cable-TV and DOCSIS fiber nodes still quote CNR, CSO and CTB, and radio-over-fiber fronthaul for mobile networks carries analog or digitised radio waveforms over short fiber spans. Modern link design mostly moves in the other direction, pushing digitisation closer to the antenna so that BER replaces CNR as the only measure. If you want to go further, search for radio-over-fiber link budget, DOCSIS fiber node CNR specification, and analog photonic link dynamic range.
